newsitem.title: GERMANY: Berlin festival quells Scientology boycott fears.
newsitem.headline: Berlin festival quells Scientology boycott fears.

text.p: The director of this year's Berlin Film Festival on Tuesday dismissed fears that Hollywood stars could boycott the event to protest at Germany's controversial treatment of the Church of Scientology.

Commenting on German radio reports of a possible protest by film stars to support fellow actors who are Scientologists, Moritz de Hadeln said he had heard nothing from U.S. studios or stars about a Berlin boycott.
"We have even asked around and there is no sign of a boycott," de Hadeln told Reuters. "It would be very stupid anyway. We've got nothing to do with that church or any other."

The 41st Berlin Film Festival, opening on February 13, will serve as a showcase for new pictures from five continents. The festival traditionally relies on a glittering array of international stars to boost its media coverage.

Several stars who attended last year -- such as Dustin Hoffman, Goldie Hawn and Oliver Stone -- were among a group of high-profile Americans who placed a full-page "Open Letter to Helmut Kohl" about Scientology in newspapers last month.
The letter condemned Germany's stance on Scientology, and compared Bonn's treatment of Scientologists to Nazi persecution of the Jews.

Germany does not accord Scientology the status of a religion, believing it to be a purely economic organisation. But Berlin officials hope the row takes a back seat and attention is focused firmly on the films when the festival gets under way.

"Smilla's Sense of Snow," one of the 25 features on the roster of competitors for the prestigious Golden Bear award, will open the festival. The Danish film based on the bestselling novel from Peter Hoeg stars British actress Julia Ormond.

Five American exports received nominations including "The Crucible" based on Arthur Miller's treatment of the Salem witch trials and "The People vs. Larry Flynt," director Milos Forman's biography of the Hustler magazine publisher.

Other contenders include "Miss Nobody", from veteran Polish director Andrzej Wajda about three girls' lives in post-communist Poland and "The Guerrillas are Tired" from Brazilian Bruno Barreto about the kidnapping of a U.S. diplomat in Rio de Janeiro in the 1960s.

The 12-day Berlinale, as the event is known, will show nearly five hundred films this year and stands just below Cannes and alongside Venice in terms of prestige on the international film festival circuit.
